title: India Just Sold Its Most Powerful Missile to a Third Country. The $630 Million Deal Rewrites the Indo-Pacific Arms Map.
excerpt: Indonesia becomes the third nation to buy the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, after the Philippines and Vietnam. India's defence exports have grown thirty-five-fold in a decade.
body:
When India and Indonesia signed a $630 million deal for BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles in Jakarta on Monday, it was more than a defence transaction. It was the clearest signal yet that India is no longer just buying weapons from the world — it is selling them, and selling them to countries that sit at the heart of the contest between Washington and Beijing for influence in the Indo-Pacific.

Indonesia is now the third country to sign on to the BrahMos programme, after the Philippines and Vietnam. All three are Southeast Asian nations with strategic coastlines, growing Chinese maritime pressure, and an appetite for deterrence that doesn't come with strings attached by either superpower. India, with its non-aligned heritage and its own fraught border history with China, is an attractive supplier.

## The Arsenal

The deal, confirmed by the Indonesian presidential palace during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's two-day visit, covers two weapons systems. The BrahMos cruise missile, jointly developed by India and Russia, is one of the fastest in the world — capable of Mach 2.8 speeds with a range of approximately 290 kilometres. It can be launched from land, sea, and air, and was used in combat for the first time during India's four-day conflict with Pakistan last year, which generated fresh international interest in the system.

Separately, Indonesia's Republikorp defence holding company and India-based Bharat Dynamics signed an agreement for the Astra beyond-visual-range air-to-air missile, which can be integrated onto the Russian-made Sukhoi fighter jets already in Indonesia's air force. This makes the package particularly cost-effective: Indonesia doesn't need to buy new aircraft to deploy the weapons.

Indian sources told Reuters the combined deal was worth approximately $630 million — nearly double the $200 million to $350 million range that was under discussion when BrahMos first entered advanced talks with Jakarta in 2023. The final contract value has not been publicly confirmed.

## Why Indonesia Matters

Indonesia is the largest economy in Southeast Asia, the world's fourth most populous country, and a sprawling archipelago of more than 17,000 islands that sits astride some of the busiest shipping lanes on Earth — including the Malacca, Sunda, and Lombok Straits.

For Indonesian military planners, the BrahMos represents a major upgrade to their coastal defence and anti-access capabilities. The Indonesian Navy previously operated the Russian-made Yakhont — an export variant of the P-800 Oniks, the missile on which the BrahMos was developed — but last fired them in exercises more than a decade ago. There is widespread speculation that Indonesia may no longer possess operational Yakhont missiles, making the BrahMos acquisition more a replacement than an addition.

The deal was signed alongside memorandums of understanding on critical minerals, steel supply chains, and agriculture. India's Steel Authority of India and Indonesia's Krakatau Steel will establish a joint venture for stainless steel slab production. The two countries also agreed to accelerate preferential trade agreement negotiations.

## A Defence Export Revolution

The BrahMos contract is the latest evidence of a structural transformation in India's defence economy. A country that for decades was the world's largest arms importer is now building a meaningful export business.

Indian defence exports, which stood at 600 crore rupees (roughly $72 million) before the Modi government took office, have surged past 21,000 crore rupees (approximately $2.5 billion). The government has notified Positive Indigenisation Lists comprising over 5,000 items that must now be manufactured domestically, and the defence startup ecosystem has expanded from roughly 400 companies to more than 120,000.

Interest in the BrahMos has grown from more than half a dozen countries, including the United Arab Emirates, following its deployment in the India-Pakistan conflict. The system's combat-proven track record — rare for a missile that hasn't been fired in anger by a major power — gives it a credibility advantage over untested competitors.

## The China Calculus

None of the parties involved in the deal mentioned China by name. But the subtext is unmistakable.

Indonesia's investment in coastal defence systems is driven in large part by Chinese maritime assertiveness in the South China Sea, where Beijing's expansive territorial claims overlap with Indonesia's exclusive economic zone around the Natuna Islands. Vietnam, the Philippines, and now Indonesia all buying BrahMos missiles creates a growing arc of Indian-made deterrence capability along China's southern maritime frontier.

For India, the strategic dividend extends beyond revenue. Every BrahMos sale deepens interoperability with a partner nation, creates long-term maintenance and training relationships, and positions New Delhi as a defence technology provider — not just a buyer — in the Indo-Pacific architecture.

"We're two of the largest democracies in the world," Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said alongside Modi. "Partnerships between us will bring benefits to the region."

Modi, for his part, said the two countries would work together on "promoting maritime safety and security in the Indian Ocean." Neither leader mentioned the BrahMos deal in their public remarks. The missile, it seems, speaks for itself.
